item.title: Microsoft identifies months-old bug as a root cause of global outage
item.description: Report identifies three factors that led to blackout: a bug, malfunctioning internal connections and server capacity Microsoft has identified the root causes of the global outage that crippled Outlook, Exchange and a host of other vital office software last week. The office software giant issued an initial report on Monday that identified three factors that led to the 24-hour blackout of its services: a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections , and server capacity. Each of these factors may have easily been resolved on their own, but, when taken together, they led to a major outage that was harder to mitigate, Microsoft executives said. Continue reading...

item.title: November 17 blackout hoax: How a conspiracy theory went viral around the world
item.description: A conspiracy theory claiming a worldwide “blackout” will hit on November 17 has spread across social media, cutting electricity, internet and banking services. The rumour stems from a routine US FEMA emergency alert test, but was amplified by cryptocurrency accounts, misleading claims about EU preparedness advice and references to The Simpsons. Recent technology outages, flight disruptions and cyberattacks have added to public anxiety, helping turn a routine test into a global blackout hoax.

item.title: The Guardian view on sporting triumphs: more than just a game | Editorial
item.description: From Welsh rugby to English football, victories on the pitch can capture a nation’s imagination and briefly make the impossible seem possible The world divides roughly in two: people who like sport and people who don’t see the point. George Orwell was roundly dismissive – “ war minus the shooting ”. Adrian Conan Doyle (Sir Arthur’s son) had the super-rationalist Sherlock Holmes baffled by why anyone should care that one horse could outrun another. Yet sport can do something that life rarely does: offer a comprehensible narrative, with a beginning, a middle and, gloriously, an end. Life is convoluted, messy and ultimately hard to assess; sport can offer resolution in 80 or 90 minutes. All of which is a long-winded way of saying: weren’t Wales magnificent in beating the All Blacks on Saturday? item.description: As hundreds of thousands of people gather in Prague to protest the Czech government's proposal to replace public broadcasting licence fees with direct state funding, Delano D'Souza is pleased to welcome Bára Stárek, Executive Director of Díky, že můžem. Stárek warns that the proposed changes offer "no real safeguards" against political influence, pointing to developments in Slovakia and Hungary. She also drew a parallel with the Velvet Revolution of 1989, recalling that "we didn't have a free media and we only had a state media" under communist rule. "Media is the first (line of) attack when you want to attack democracy," she said. With the legislation expected to reach Parliament in January, Stárek believes the demonstrations will continue if the government refuses to engage in any discussions.

item.title: Anthropic recognises the risks to humanity – but is its governance really up to the job? | Nils Pratley
item.description: The Claude AI developer’s unique setup is supposedly high-minded, but still represents extraordinary power concentration Boardroom governance matters, even in the world of big tech, it turns out. The business of how companies are run, investors are discovering, can be more complicated than handing the founder or superstar chief executive as much control as he wants (it’s usually a he) and waiting for brilliant returns to appear. Sometimes a few checks on power are useful, especially when a crisis strikes. This revelation is no revelation at all, of course. For about 30 years until the first generation of big US tech companies came along, the thrust of corporate governance thinking was to insist on the basic fairness of the principle of “one share, one vote”. The owners should be able to chuck out misbehaving or underperforming managers by a simple majority, in other words. Continue reading...

item.title: Quel head trip! Failed postcards, scrapping poets and germ-ridden film rock Paris Photo – review
item.description: Grand Palais, Paris The fair celebrated the bicentenary of photography – but did anyone care? Especially when the most compelling images proposed whole new ways of seeing No one at the three-day Paris Photo fair seemed worried about being a target for protesters – the fate of fellow art fair Art Basel Paris, which closed two days early. “Photography isn’t expensive enough,” joked one gallerist. This 29th edition coincided with celebrations across France of the bicentenary of photography, and as such looked back at photography’s origins and the questions that have preoccupied photographers from the beginning. One example was a 19th-century portrait that is thought to be an extremely rare depiction of Rimbaud with a black eye – the poet was a known ruffian who often got physical over literary squabbles. Whether the photograph is really Rimbaud or not begs the question: what matters more, the truth, or what we believe the truth to be? After 200 years, photography hasn’t resolved the issue

item.title: Hero, villain or victim: why are refugees so rarely seen now as fully human? | Zoe Williams
item.description: The understanding of refugees as complex individuals, motivated variously by wanting to build a new life and return to what was theirs, often seems to have been lost. A new film offers a different, truer, perspective There was a screening last week of Seize the Summit, which follows four refugees as they try to reach the top of Kilimanjaro. It was organised by a recent MA graduate from Goldsmiths, with a panel afterwards, which I was set to chair. So she and I were spitballing what the film-maker, Arwa Damon, would want to talk about, and Hanya, the graduate, said: “I think her purpose is to mainstream the idea of the refugee as a human being.” It was such a stark statement that we both started laughing. There are many categories of refugee in current affairs storytelling. There’s the desperate victim; the criminal, or criminal-waiting-to-happen; the hero, battling unimaginable odds, though this tends to be a retrospective narrative, ie second-generation members of a diaspora talking a

item.title: Russia's war on Ukraine: 'Americans want to have a deal whatever the cost for both Ukraine & Europe'
item.description: Delano D'Souza is pleased to welcome Grégoire Roos, Director of the Europe and Russia and Eurasia Programmes at Chatham House. As European countries prepare to take part in the next round of Ukraine peace talks, Roos questions whether having five European representatives could weaken their negotiating position. "The other option is to realize that it dilutes the negotiating power of Europe. And I would lean towards that," he says, proposing Finnish President Alexander Stubb as a possible representative. Roos also points to differences between Washington and European governments over negotiations with Russia. While "the Americans do absolutely want to have a deal whatever the cost for both Ukraine and Europe," he argues that European governments have little choice but to maintain pressure on Moscow, which has yet to abandon its "maximalist demands."

It is a melancholy satire on caste shame, sexual politics and land exploitation in the Philippines, symbolised by a private golf course in Manila, an artificial landscape as depthless and surreal as the gardens in Last Year in Marienbad . Irrigating the vivid greens and undulating fairways requires oceans of precious water – water that, in the course of one unbearable heatwave, is rationed for the sweating lower orders in the city, way beyond the golf club’s luxurious precincts. item.title: The hill I will die on: There is only one acceptable occasion on which to ghost someone – when you die | Temi Wilkey
item.description: Dystopian dating on apps is more Thatcherite horror story than love story. Romance that blossoms through community and human connection needs a renaissance Digitising our dating lives has conditioned us all away from human connection. I spend weeks of my life huffing and puffing to keep the balloon of flirty banter in the air – with a stranger I only find vaguely attractive. I go on dates with people who are “my type on paper” but upon meeting, find the paper much better than the person. I meet a woman with a devastating mouth and an even more devastating wit, only for her to ghost . The only acceptable reason to ghost someone is if you have, in fact, died. Long ago, when Margaret Thatcher proclaimed “There is no such thing as society”, she wasn’t heralding an era of Tory rule that destroyed all public services that kept true community alive. No – she was prophesying 40 years into the future about the digital-age phenomenon of ghosting. The fact that this practice is widespread enough

He’s dead, or close to it, having come round from an emergency heart bypass in his 52nd year only to find himself sinking into a deep pool of warm gloop with honey-coloured light flowing at him from all directions. A disembodied voice calling itself Charles has offered him a choice that is hinted at but so far unspecified. What we do know is that before he makes his choice, Michael – a rock star who had three Top 10 hits in the UK and once danced in an LA disco with Björk and Courtney Love – is invited to revisit a single year of his life. item.title: The one change that worked: I was burnt out and lonely – until I started ice skating
item.description: I was stressed and newly diagnosed with ADHD when I decided to choose a new hobby. It awakened my playfulness and immediately improved my quality of life In 2024, I decided to return to England after four and a half years in Lisbon. My first winter back in the UK was psychologically challenging. Working alone on my next book didn’t feel as enjoyable in cold, grey London as it had abroad. The 10th anniversary of my father’s death was approaching and I felt a profound loneliness which, much like the cold, began to seep into my bones. I was struggling, too, to readjust to London’s cost and pace of living. During this time, I was diagnosed with combined-type attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). I used to think I was depressed, but my diagnosis made me realise that part of how I felt was burnout – my brain’s ability to regulate stress was depleted. I felt overwhelmed and would shut down, which would lead to cycles of anxiety, depression and self-criticism. Continue reading...

item.title: The pet I’ll never forget: Mr Baxter, who ate our belongings – and broke our hearts
item.description: Reared on a puppy farm, and abandoned by a previous owner, he was half-starved when we adopted him. But he grew strong, chomping through everything from dog beds to sunglasses and my debut book The day we brought our 14-week-old cocker spaniel home in 2022, I was wearing a silk scarf I’d picked up decades ago in a vintage shop in Tokyo. I didn’t know it then but that rainy afternoon would be the last time I’d wear it. Three days later, it was in my new puppy’s mouth. Once he’d finished tearing my scarf to shreds, he gazed at me with soulful chocolate brown eyes, fluttering his long eyelashes. No matter how fond I was of that silk scarf, how could I be angry? Puppies chew stuff. That’s what they do. Mr Baxter gnawed his way through four dog beds, blankets and multiple dog leads. Nothing was off-limits. Socks, shoes, trainers, gloves, flat caps, berets, the freshly printed chapters of my debut book, a nifty pair of 70s sunglasses. Fearless and lithe, he grabbed things we naively thought

item.description: Meanwhile, severe thunderstorms bring hailstones the size of baseballs in Argentina The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989. Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. item.title: Not All Those Who Wander Are Lost album review – Anna Lapwood journeys to middle earth
item.description: Lapwood/Nidaros Cathedral Girls’ Choir (Sony) Lapwood has turned Howard Shore’s film score into an impressive full-blown organ symphony When a fan requested she play Concerning Hobbits from The Lord of the Rings, little did Anna Lapwood imagine that she would go on to spend a year turning Howard Shore’s leitmotif-led soundtrack into a full-blown organ symphony. Remarkably, she transcribed all but one segment by ear, a feat in itself. That she manages to tell the story chronologically over a 38-minute, three-movement span is equally impressive. But wait, there’s more. Reckoning the symphony would benefit from the human voice, she incorporated a handful of songs, performing them live – in Tolkien’s Elvish dialect – while playing the Nidaros Cathedral organ in Trondheim, Norway. The results are frequently convincing, though the folksy music of the Shire is less effective on the organ than the baleful music of Sauron and the Ringwraiths. That afternoon, she called her manager Kat. “I told her: ‘I’ve thrown a brick through the window at Spotify.’ She went: ‘What, literally?’ and I said: ‘No, but I’ve been standing outside their offices with a megaphone, so that relationship is over. There he chose fabric, before flying to Hong Kong to be fitted for four shirts, and on to Tokyo, where he was measured by master tailor Yuhei Yamamoto and master shoe­maker Yohei Fukuda. And guess what? The world’s finest craftsmen will give you all that – though Shteyngart, who emigrated from Leningrad to the US in 1979, argues that a great suit serves a deeper need than vanity. item.title: ‘A songbook for protest movements’: how did this secret mission to smuggle antifascist music out of Spain ever get forgotten?
item.description: In 1961, a group of Italian creatives crossed the border to collect anti-Franco resistance songs and share them with the world – sparking intense backlash from the dictator. A new documentary retraces that perilous journey In the summer of 1961, four Italians crossed the Pyrenees into fascist Spain. Unknown to the border guards, their car was loaded with microfilm, a tape recorder and, tucked in the pocket of a writer and musician named Sergio Liberovici, a book of matches – each split in half, etched with the addresses of Spanish antifascists in miniature and glued back together, a hairline fracture concealing secrets that, if discovered, could result in jail or worse. Along with Michele Luciano Straniero, Emilio Jona and Margherita Galante Garrone, Liberovici was a member of a leftwing collective named Cantacronache. item.description: The head of Women’s Aid has a unique insight into the ways technology provides mechanisms for abuse. She discusses online predators, the UK’s early release scheme – and why the fastest growing cohort of domestic abusers is young men At last Tuesday’s all-staff meeting for Women’s Aid there was an unfamiliar undercurrent of optimism. It is a feeling that is very unusual when you have about 85 people working in the domestic violence sector gathered in one room. Staff were feeling encouraged by the sentencing of Russell Brand a day earlier, and also cheered by Channel 4’s announcement at the start of the month that it would stop making Married at First Sight, a programme the charity had campaigned against, calling out “multiple incidents where women have [been] subjected to abuse and manipulation” on these kinds of reality dating shows. item.title: Midnight Diner: Netflix just dropped its most beautiful show in years … and it’s barely been noticed
item.description: Disarmingly thoughtful stillness is the order of the day in the latest season of this Japanese show about a Tokyo eatery. What a shame it feels buried under other content The first time we see the Master (Kaoru Kobayashi) in the sixth season of Midnight Diner, he cuts a curiously morose figure. His usually bustling establishment – open from midnight to 7am – is empty. No one, he notes, will come: Covid-19 keeps them at home. An ironic start for a drama arriving after a seven-year absence, delayed in part by uncertainty over the pandemic’s impact on small eateries. The show’s return isn’t a shock. Based on Yarō Abe’s long-running manga, it has been a TV fixture in Japan since 2009. Netflix has just quietly released it, buried by the platform’s seeming aversion to marketing non-English series, which has swallowed reams of remarkable Japanese television. Continue reading...

item.title: Kindness of strangers: I was stranded, dressed as a flapper, on a freezing night. Then a cheerful taxi driver pulled over
item.description: My tyre was blown so he changed it for me. When I offered payment he said, ‘Don’t be ridiculous, love’ Read more in the kindness of strangers series I had to fight not to lose control of the car. I was in my early 20s and driving home from a fancy dress party when bang – my tyre suddenly blew. I managed to wrestle my Toyota Corolla to a stop without crashing and sat there, heart pounding, as I wondered what to do next. It was 1982 in Canberra; a foggy, bitterly cold night in the middle of winter. I was wearing a silly flapper dress and high heels – I’m not sure I’d even packed a jacket! I had a spare tyre in the back but little idea how to change it. My options were to make the one-hour walk home alone or wait to see if another car passed and could offer me a ride. For 30 minutes I sat in the driver’s seat helplessly, unsure what to do. Continue reading...

item.title: Gout is on the rise – and excruciating. Why are sufferers still judged for it?
item.description: About 1.6 million people in the UK have this agonising condition, but it is often viewed as a comical malady brought on by overconsumption and idleness. What can be done to end the stigma? Brett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. When he described the episode to his family, they suggested it might be gout. “I was like, really?” he says. “Can you get that in your 30s?” Continue reading...

item.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto Flu’: is the whole world really taking the day off work to play GTA VI?
item.description: Headlines have claimed the release of the first new GTA game in 13 years will hugely affect the global economy on Thursday – but there’s another story that’s been left behind A new pandemic is threatening planet Earth. It’s scheduled to hit 19 November. Entire offices and worksites will be emptied; employees struck down by a mysterious illness. But you need not panic: it isn’t fatal. It should pass in a few days. The anticipation for Grand Theft Auto VI, the first new game in the franchise in 13 years, is so high that a steady stream of news coverage has suggested it heralds economic catastrophe due to workers taking time off to play the game. The term “GTA Flu” was coined for the swathe of sickies that reportedly happened when GTA V was released in 2013, and – supposedly – are set to happen again when GTA VI comes out this week. item.title: Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained

item.description: A new film starring Helen Mirren explores the Ripley writer’s later years, but was she really so rude and eccentric? Editors and publishers who worked with her look back Publisher and bookseller Otto Penzler has loved Patricia Highsmith’s work all his life, but their first meeting was a washout. In 1984, she agreed to give a reading at The Mysterious Bookshop, his store on West 56th Street in New York. The American author of the Ripley novels, then 63, had lived in Europe for 20 years – in England, then France, then Switzerland – and seldom made public appearances, so he had high hopes. “But no one showed up. We had maybe four people,” Penzler says from his book-lined office under the shop. Now 84, with a tidy white beard and a warm, amused manner, he is just back from a crime fiction convention and still very much in the game. item.description: After a childhood of grief, hardship and hunger, the Guardian food writer’s father Raj always resisted going back to Uganda. What happened when he finally agreed to accompany her on a bittersweet journey into the past? The moment I step off the plane and on to the soil of Entebbe it hits me. Uganda is in my blood. This country that had once existed only in my imagination is finally real. The heat is heavy, the earth bright and rich like dark terracotta. I want to capture this moment – me with my 75-year-old dad, back where he was born. A place he never imagined he would return to. It later transpired that they thought I was turning 41. But even then to receive nothing is hurtful . They blamed it on old age and said they had been struggling with their health. item.description: Heavy rain and strong winds have also caused disruption across British Columbia, Canada, over the last week Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninsula this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm (13.97in) in 12 hours. In Lisbon, 183 flights were cancelled on Wednesday, about a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations. After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. item.title: ‘To them, we’re just NPCs’: the artists and activists challenging Trump’s video game propaganda
item.description: Order a Diet Coke or invade Iran – that’s the choice facing the US president in one of several satirical games, as designers turn the gamification of politics back on the White House In early September, the Trump White House announced a surprising new addition to its official website. Named simply Arcade , it is a collection of browser games based on classic titles such as Flappy Bird, Snake, and Tetris, but re-tuned as flagrant works of political propaganda. Designed to court reactionary gamers, they push the administration’s policies on immigration and other hot-button issues, while dehumanising their targets. There have recently been some new additions: a Temple Run clone named Red Scare about crossing the “ration market” and escaping the Democratic Socialists of America, and another simple item-matching game about the threat of socialism. item.title: A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding
item.description: A sweeping analysis of 540 million years of marine fossils has revealed surprising gaps in our understanding of Earth's ancient life. Scientists discovered that some of the greatest opportunities for finding previously unknown species lie in relatively recent geological periods, rather than the distant past. By mapping unexplored fossil-rich regions around the world, researchers have created a powerful tool to guide future excavations.

item.title: A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets

Hidden ultraviolet wing patterns and DNA differences revealed the truth, leaving scientists puzzled about how the butterflies remain genetically separate despite living side by side.

item.title: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer review – an adorable raccoon mends the world, one parcel at a time
item.description: Nintendo Switch/2, PlayStation 4/5, Xbox One/series X/S, PC; Denkiworks/Inpleron Limited This gentle game of fixing and fetching, in which you play as a furry post office worker on a BMX, has a slow, calming magic that delights in routine and restoration Arriving alongside November’s blue wave , Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is a game of quiet restoration that feels perfectly suited to the current moment. Tasked with repairing an ancient shrine in the weeks leading up to a local festival, you’ll find yourself cleaning out trash, mending broken arches and slowly bringing a small rural community back together. It sounds a bit like JL Carr’s compact but enchanting novel A Month in the Country , except instead of shell-shocked veterans of the first world war you’re left exploring the rich inner life of a Japanese racoon dog who can ride a BMX. Even so, the mixture of steady progress and general low stakes proves intoxicating. This is a short game, but it’s hard not to linger over it. Continue readi

item.title: Earth's fiery birth may have created hundreds of oceans' worth of water
item.description: Earth's water may have been born in the planet's fiery atmosphere rather than delivered by icy comets or asteroids. Scientists discovered that rocky pebbles reacting with hydrogen under extreme heat can produce water in minutes, potentially generating hundreds of oceans' worth during Earth's formation. The findings suggest that water may be a natural part of how rocky planets form, rather than something that must arrive from space.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03636-5 A fresh approach considers waist circumference, rather than just weight and height, providing a more accurate classification.

item.title: New culprit in early Alzheimer’s: blood–brain barrier blocks protective proteins
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03655-2 The brain relies on crucial proteins to maintain neurons. This system is disrupted in mice with neurological disease.

item.title: AI’s energy paradox: will the AI boom strain energy systems or be the source of solutions?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03412-5 Ginelle Greene-Dewasmes is leading a community of interdisciplinary specialists exploring how to make the energy use of artificial intelligence net-positive.

item.title: Retractions of old papers are on the rise: when should bad science be culled?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03624-9 Decades-old papers are increasingly being pulled from the literature, bringing a host of challenges.

item.title: Author or just ‘acknowledged’? How women are not gaining full credit for research
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03448-7 An analysis of who is more likely to get authorship than acknowledgement highlights the influence of a researcher’s gender and status.

item.title: Engineered bacteria are weaning farms away from synthetic fertilizers
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03641-8 Scientists are editing microbes to supply more nitrogen to staple crops.

item.title: Proposed approach for diagnosing obesity outperforms old method
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03425-0 A framework for diagnosing obesity that was proposed in 2025 incorporates waist circumference and related measures and distinguishes clinical from preclinical obesity on the basis of obesity-induced organ dysfunction. In an international multi-cohort study of 844,108 adults, this framework outperformed conventional body-mass-index-based criteria in diagnosing obesity and stratifying mortality risk.

item.title: Personal incentives for public officials drove a drop in China’s fertility
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03274-x Once the promotion prospects of bureaucrats became tied to birth targets, the country’s one-child policy became more effective. Can the state now reverse this effect?

item.title: Can green technologies deliver energy security in an unstable world?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03409-0 As global energy markets grapple with a period of sustained political volatility, researchers are digging deep for solutions.

item.title: Human replisomes direct a dedicated leading-strand primase for fork restart
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11204-0 Structural and biochemical studies show that the CMG helicase directly recruits PRIMPOL for leading-strand repriming, enabling replication fork restart and limiting post-replicative DNA gaps.

item.title: Bureaucratic incentives shaped effectiveness of the one-child policy in China
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11232-w Stronger bureaucratic incentives under China’s one vote veto policy intensified enforcement of the one-child policy, accounting for nearly half of China’s fertility decline during the 1990s.

item.title: Validation of clinical and preclinical obesity across global cohorts
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11237-5 A large-scale data analysis assesses the Lancet Commission’s proposed diagnostic framework for obesity, finding that this framework, in which BMI is combined with other criteria, such as waist circumference and organ function, is more useful than classifications based on BMI alone.

item.title: UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11256-2 TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact and suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication; a therapeutic strategy is found that corrects UNC13A cryptic splicing by using splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides.

item.title: NRF2 is a mechanosensitive checkpoint for NLRP3 inflammasome activation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11324-7 The stiffness of the extracellular matrix is identified as a pivotal factor that influences activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in vitro and in vivo.

item.title: Non-halogen aqueous electrolytes for four-electron iodine conversion
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11282-0 An electrolyte framework that harnesses anionic chemistry to coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions enables reversible four-electron iodine conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes, and is validated in metal–iodine batteries.

item.title: Bistable regulation of adipocyte heterogeneity governs thermogenesis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11308-7 IL-1β from neutrophils and macrophages stabilizes nearby brown adipocytes in a low-UCP1 state; cold temperature reduces IL-1β via sympathetic nerves, leading to transition to a high-UCP1 state and increased thermogenesis, while higher temperatures have the opposite effect.

item.title: Epigenetic heterogeneity in breast tumours informs diagnosis and prognosis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11230-y Single-cell epigenetic analyses reveal a conserved epigenetic signature across patients that may help identify those at increased risk for disease relapse in breast cancer.

item.title: A plant RNA-binding protein senses 2′,3′-cNMP produced by insect effectors
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11259-z The rice RNA-binding protein NIB1 detects 2′,3′-cyclic nucleotide products from insect saliva RNase, forming nuclear condensates that recruit EDS1 to activate defence, revealing a conserved messenger-based immune pathway in plants.

item.title: Flexible rubber blades for tidal turbines
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11278-w Flexible tidal turbine blades with passive trailing-edge deformation match the energy yield of active pitch-controlled blades while reducing fatigue-inducing load fluctuations by up to one-third, lowering maintenance complexity.

item.title: Hadean mantle depletion and 3.95-Gyr subduction implied by North China rocks
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11280-2 Analysis of a 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss from eastern Hebei, China, reveals a composition suggesting a low-temperature altered basaltic source, that originated from a mantle depleted in the Hadean, was most likely transported to mantle depths through a transient subduction event and partially melted to produce the trondhjemite.

item.title: Human land use drives microplastic abundance in terrestrial wildlife
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11285-x Microplastic burdens in Brazilian tapirs and anteaters rise with human-modified land use and proximity to development, however animals in remote habitats also carry microplastics, showing that landscape change and individual space use jointly shape wildlife exposure.

item.title: Transient nuclear softening for zygotic gene activation in mice
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11240-w A distinct physical nuclear state acquired by embryos at the beginning of life supports the initiation of the zygotic transcription program.

item.title: Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11264-2 Experiments in mouse models show that immunoglobulin A in the gut lumen has a role in regulating the turnover of colon epithelial cells and reduces the susceptibility of mice to colorectal cancer.

item.title: Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11269-x The somatic evolutionary histories of haematopoietic cells in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia diagnosis show that the clonal dynamics of blood comply with a set of simple evolutionary rules.

item.title: Scale-rich network-based metamaterials
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11191-2 A network-science-based framework that embeds network heterogeneity into mechanical metamaterials is used to produce scale-rich metamaterials that exhibit properties inaccessible to traditional single-scale systems.

item.title: The molecular basis of replication fork restart via repriming by PRIMPOL
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11276-y PRIMPOL is recruited to stalled forks through an interaction with the replicative helicase CDC45–MCM2–7–GINS, facilitating primer handover from PRIMPOL to the high-fidelity polymerase ε, minimizing mutagenic DNA synthesis.

item.title: Domain-alteration chimeras rewire oncogenic complexes in prostate cancer
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11262-4 A novel therapeutic modality enforces non-native androgen receptor (AR)–p300/CBP interactions to collapse AR transcriptional programs, producing super-inhibitory, lineage-selective suppression of metastatic prostate cancer and establishing domain-alteration chimeras as a broadly applicable therapeutic strategy leveraging induced proximity.

item.title: Glycosylation and importins liquefy the FG barrier in live nuclear pores
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11258-0 Nuclear pore proteins maintain a fluid, spatially organized barrier through coordinated molecular interactions, explaining how cells achieve selective transport and reconciling competing models of pore structure.

item.title: Severe drought and warming increase the extinction risk of cacti
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11265-1 Severe drought and warming will substantially increase the loss of suitable climatic area for cactus species.

item.title: Low-power 2D CFETs using single-crystal high-κ dielectrics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11272-2 A transferable single-crystal anatase titanium dioxide dielectric enables high-quality interfaces with two-dimensional semiconductors, yielding near-ideal switching, low hysteresis and ultra-low-power complementary transistors and inverters.

item.title: Independent interferometric observable confirms black hole shadow in M87*
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11241-9 An imaging algorithm using closure-invariant formalism and diffusion-based reconstruction applied to supermassive black hole very long baseline radio interferometry datasets enables independent recovery of the ring-like shadow and mass that is free from the usual calibration and imaging assumptions.

item.title: Mitochondrial protein import defects enhance tumour immunogenicity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11249-1 Inhibition of mitochondrial protein import can enhance tumour immunogenicity by promoting mitochondrial DNA release.

item.title: Manchester City’s weaknesses under Enzo Maresca are being exposed

After seven straight wins from the start of the season, that’s now three straight defeats, a pattern so unusual that it’s been recorded only once before in top-flight English history, by Sheffield Wednesday in 1904-05. The three defeats were all different, Maresca said, although in all of them City had had more possession and more chances. In the 2-1 defeat at Aston Villa two weeks ago, City had 63% of the ball and had 15 chances to Villa’s eight. In the 1-0 home defeat to Brighton last weekend, they had 62% possession and 21 chances to seven. At the City Ground, it was 79% possession and 12 chances to 11. item.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action
item.description: Delap’s talents resurface in style, Gómez delights Brighton with more fireworks, and hair-pulling confusion at Everton It would have been very easy for Oliver Glasner to lose patience with Liam Delap. The forward is still only 23, yet the days when he was rattling in 12 in a Premier League season for Ipswich have come to seem a very long time ago (and his six games for Manchester City even longer). A season at Chelsea had left him bereft of confidence, an odd mix of diffidence and overaggression, devoid of composure in the box, arms flailing like a broken windmill. But the old gifts have not left him. Both goals on Saturday were the result of great muscular surges and if the first finish seemed essentially about hitting the ball as hard as possible on target, the second was a precise – and still powerful – finish in off the far post. After games such as this it’s possible to imagine him as England’s long-term replacement for Harry Kane. Jonathan Wilson Match report: Nottingham Forest 3

item.description: Teenage ultras are increasingly causing disorder and communities fear it will not be long before it becomes something more dangerous It is five past three on Saturday afternoon and the teenage ultras of Hednesford Town are running late. They have arrived in Chester for their team’s National League North fixture and have hailed taxis, determined to make their presence felt at the ground. But word appears to have got out about their arrival. As one car turns away from the city’s charming half-timbered houses and into narrow residential streets, half a dozen local youths appear, haring round the corner in balaclavas. They try to attack the cab and chase after it as it pulls away. The smell of pyro is everywhere. As the taxi finally gets clear, the Chester gang stops in the middle of the road, shouting and gesticulating. One lad, no older than 16, pulls a long blade from inside his trousers and brandishes it. item.title: Billions in revenue proves Fifa right on the World Cup – but only on things it cares about
item.description: The 2026 edition of the tournament brought in untold amounts of money to Gianni Infantino’s governing body The total hasn’t entirely stopped rising yet, still clicking away towards a final tally. Still, Fifa has already announced that it surpassed its own lofty revenue projections for the 2026 World Cup, bringing in $15bn, significantly more than anticipated. It appears that a third of that total – $5bn – came from ticket sales and hospitality alone, per reporting from the Times . That would mean direct income from the matchgoing fans came in five times as high in the United States, Canada and Mexico as it did at the last World Cup, in Qatar in 2022, when the total stood at $929m. While 2026’s expanded World Cup added 40 games to the schedule, the takings nevertheless went from an average of about $14.5m per match to about $48m. Continue reading...

item.description: Club’s predicament raises interesting questions about principles, both for individuals and the Premier League I felt unbelievably ponderous. My head was made of Aztec stone. I realised I didn’t want to be with all these people. Somebody came at me, a huge individual in silver and blue. I fell at his feet and grabbed one shoe. I started untying the lace. He kicked away from me. I got up and walked off. I was exceedingly hungry. Not my words. Also not the words of the Manchester City centre-back Marc Guéhi, despite what you were thinking there. The stadium announcer hollered out the first names of Borussia Dortmund’s starting lineup and the supporters responded with their last names, tens of thousands of voices bellowing as one. item.title: Mourinho’s plan comes together as Real Madrid relaunch with clásico statement | Sid Lowe
item.description: It was just like old times as José Mourinho ended a night at Camp Nou with a knee slide and three points José Mourinho had already done the por qu é? , the printout and the press conference no-show in under 100 days. Now he’s done a knee slide too, and in the perfect place: back where it all began and where it can all begin again. When Kylian Mbappé scored the first in the clásico on Sunday night, Real Madrid’s manager hardly moved, sitting in the shadow of the bench – but when the striker got the second to win it with time running out, that was different. Mourinho leapt into the light, throwing himself to the grass, the knees of a 63-year-old’s trousers muddy as a schoolboy’s, stuck his tongue out and pumped his fists. He does so love it when a plan comes together. To the right of him, the bench was emptying, subs joining the players in sprinting towards the south-west corner. item.title: Ian Holloway’s circus: why the manager’s antics are no laughing matter for fans
item.description: Swindon manager has a history of viral outbursts but fans want a united club and manager they can support In Ian Holloway’s often madcap managerial orbit, this was simply the latest in a steady succession of eccentric outbursts. Eyes bulging as he spoke, he boomed the letter “D” and promptly stabbed himself in the chest with an imaginary dagger. Next came the letter “M” alongside a blow from another invisible knife. Finally, a “W” followed by a jab to the heart. “Dead. Man. Walking,” he declared, pausing for effect between words and briefly falling into an Oscar-worthy zombie stupor. “That’s how it feels.” To an offbeat press conference genre containing seagulls following trawlers and self-proclaimed special ones, it was a crazy new entry worthy of its subsequent viral nature. Holloway at his finest. Continue reading...

item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. item.description: Get our roundup of women’s football for free twice a week, featuring the insights of experts such as Ada Hegerberg and Magdalena Eriksson Join us as we delve deeper into the wonderful world of women’s football in our weekly newsletter. It is informative, entertaining, global, critical – when needed – and, above all, passionate. Written mainly by Júlia Belas Trindade and Sophie Downey , expect guest appearances from stars such as Anita Asante, Ada Hegerberg and many more. Try our other sports emails: as well as the occasionally funny football email The Fiver from Monday to Friday, there are weekly catch-ups for cricket in The Spin and rugby union in The Breakdown , and our seven-day roundup of the best of our sports journalism in The Recap .
